e-means Clustering

Source: R/emeans.R
shoal_emeans.Rd

k-means fitted by e-means (Bessa et al. 2026), via an in-tree Rust port of the reference implementation in faiss (Meta FAIR). Lloyd's algorithm, behind shoal_kmeans(), recomputes every centroid from all the data at each iteration. e-means instead visits the data in random mini-batches and moves each centroid towards its batch mean by an exponential moving average. The batch size and step size come from scaling laws the authors fitted on the number of rows, clusters and passes. It minimises the same within-cluster sum of squares, and with many rows and hundreds of clusters or more it reaches the loss of a converged k-means in a handful of passes over the data.

Usage

shoal_emeans(
  x,
  k,
  epochs = 5,
  metric = c("euclidean", "cosine"),
  batch_law = c("auto", "throughput", "quality"),
  batch_size = NULL,
  alpha0 = NULL,
  revive_threshold = NULL,
  seed = 1L
)

Arguments

x

A numeric matrix or data frame. Data frames are coerced to a matrix using their numeric columns (non-numeric columns are dropped).

k

Number of clusters. Must be at least 1 and no more than nrow(x).

epochs

Number of passes over the data, the training budget, at most 1000. A fractional value visits a random fraction of the rows in one of the passes. Default 5, as upstream.

metric

"euclidean" (default) for k-means, or "cosine" for spherical k-means on directions; see the Cosine mode section.

batch_law

Which fitted law sets the batch size when batch_size is not given: "auto" (default), "throughput" or "quality".

batch_size

Rows per update, capped at nrow(x). NULL (default) uses the batch law.

alpha0

Initial step of the moving average, in \((0, 1]\). NULL (default) uses the step law at the batch size in use.

revive_threshold

Revive clusters whose running mass falls below this fraction of the mean mass; 0 turns revival off. NULL (default) uses 0.1, or 0 for data with at most two columns, where upstream found revival costs accuracy.

seed

Non-negative whole-number seed for the start, the batch order and revival. Stored and passed as a double, so values beyond the integer range are safe. Default 1L.

Value

An object of class c("shoal_emeans", "shoal_kmeans", "shoal_clustering"): a list with components cluster (integer vector of cluster IDs), n_clusters, n_noise (always 0), data, algorithm, params, metric, centroids (a k x ncol(x) matrix), inertia, sizes, epoch_objective, n_splits and recipe.

epoch_objective gives, per epoch, the sum of squared distances from the rows visited to the centroids they were assigned against. Those centroids move during the epoch, so it is a record of training, not the final error. n_splits counts revivals, and a cluster can be revived more than once. recipe is the plan used: batch_law, which is NA when batch_size was given, batch_size, alpha0, epoch_rows (rows visited per epoch), total_steps and revive_threshold.

When to use it

e-means is for scale: many rows and many clusters. Typical uses are a codebook for vector quantisation, a fixed set of centroids that stands in for every vector nearest to it, and a fine partition of an embedding collection. The scaling laws were fitted on \(10^5\) to \(10^8\) rows and 256 to 65,536 clusters. Outside that range e-means still runs, but its settings are not tuned there. On small data with few clusters, prefer shoal_kmeans(). Its restarts, ten by default, guard against the poor local minima that a single random start can settle in, and e-means makes one random start.

The cost is fixed by epochs: one pass over the data per epoch, plus one for the final assignment. There are no restarts and no convergence test.

Results do not depend on where the data sits. Euclidean mode works relative to the column means, so projected coordinates far from the origin cluster as well as local ones.

Cosine mode

metric = "cosine" is spherical k-means, for embedding vectors compared by cosine similarity. Rows are scaled to unit length internally, each is assigned to the centroid of largest cosine similarity, and the centroids are unit vectors. Rescaling rows therefore has no effect. A row of all zeros has no direction and is an error. inertia is then the sum of squared distances between the unit rows and their unit centroids, \(\sum 2(1 - \cos\theta)\).

The training plan

Unless given, the batch size and the initial step alpha0 come from the fitted laws. The step then falls along half a cosine curve to a tenth of alpha0 by the end of the run. batch_law = "quality" uses batches about eight times smaller than "throughput", trading speed for a lower final loss; "auto" chooses "quality" for data with at most 16 columns and "throughput" above, as upstream does.

Each centroid carries a running mass, a moving average of the number of rows assigned to it. Every five updates, clusters whose mass has fallen below revive_threshold times the mean mass are revived: a donor drawn in proportion to its mass is split in two, and one half takes the place of the starved cluster. The plan used is returned in recipe.

Assignments

The centroids are the means of the rows assigned to them during the final training epoch, scaled to unit length in cosine mode. One exact pass then assigns each row to its nearest final centroid, so cluster, inertia and sizes describe the partition the centroids induce, and predict() on the training data reproduces cluster. The reference implementation saves that pass and returns the labels from the last training epoch, during which the centroids were still moving. A centroid can end the run with no points. sizes then has a zero for it, and n_clusters counts only the clusters with points.

Reproducibility

As in shoal_kmeans(), seed is a parameter rather than being taken from R's RNG. The same seed, parameters and data give identical results whatever the thread count. Between machines, results can differ by rounding, because the matrix-product kernel is chosen for the CPU, and a row at a near-tie between two centroids can then change cluster. A seed does not reproduce a run of the reference implementation, whose random streams differ; the port is checked against it with the start, the batch order and the random draws fixed instead.

References

Bessa, S., Mazaré, P.-E., Szilvasy, G., Touvron, H., Picard, D., Douze, M. and Jégou, H. (2026). e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs). arXiv:2611.09501. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09501

Reference implementation: faiss.contrib.e_means, https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/tree/main/contrib/e_means

See also

shoal_kmeans() for Lloyd's algorithm with k-means++ restarts, and predict.shoal_kmeans() for assigning new observations.

Examples

set.seed(1)
centres <- matrix(rnorm(40 * 8, sd = 4), ncol = 8)
x <- centres[sample.int(40, 20000, replace = TRUE), ] +
  matrix(rnorm(20000 * 8), ncol = 8)

fit <- shoal_emeans(x, k = 40L)
fit
#> 
#> ── e-means Clustering 
#> Metric: "euclidean"
#> Parameters: k = 40, epochs = 5, batch_law = auto, seed = 1
#> Clusters: 40, Noise points: 0
#> Within-cluster sum of squares: 259590
#> Cluster sizes: min 227, median 498, max 1062
#> Training: 5 epochs, 785 updates of 128 rows (quality batch law), initial step
#> 0.116, 3 revivals
fit$recipe$batch_size
#> [1] 128
predict(fit, x[1:5, ])
#> [1] 17 14  2 30 28

# Spherical k-means, clustering directions.
shoal_emeans(x, k = 40L, metric = "cosine")
#> 
#> ── e-means Clustering 
#> Metric: "cosine"
#> Parameters: k = 40, epochs = 5, batch_law = auto, seed = 1
#> Clusters: 40, Noise points: 0
#> Within-cluster sum of squares: 2351.2
#> Cluster sizes: min 217, median 500.5, max 1033
#> Training: 5 epochs, 785 updates of 128 rows (quality batch law), initial step
#> 0.116, 2 revivals
